title: How the U.S. Military Draft Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the U.S. military draft (conscription): the Selective Service System's registration requirement for men 18 to 25, who is exempt, how the draft lottery works, the induction and exemption process, conscientious objector classifications, the all-volunteer force debate with pros and cons, and the history of the draft from Vietnam through Lewis Hershey's deferment policy and Robert McNamara's New Standards program. The episode closes with a listener mail from Noah in Scotland about the Shanghai Tower.

segments.title: Opening banter and personal draft registration
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the bureaucracy-themed episode, discuss registering for Selective Service, and Josh's father's draft history during Vietnam. They touch on a Genghis Khan mention and the film Mongol.

segments.title: Draft history around the world
segments.summary: The hosts note conscription dates back to ancient China and that most civilizations have used drafts. The U.S. has had drafts in the Civil War era, the War of 1812, World War I, World War II, and Vietnam (1961 to 1973). Opposition to the Vietnam draft was the first major backlash.

segments.title: Current U.S. military and the Selective Service System
segments.summary: The U.S. has an all-volunteer military of about 1.31 million active duty and about 815,000 reservists. A draft would require the President and Congress to act. Jimmy Carter reactivated Selective Service in 1980 after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Selective Service maintains a database of men aged 18 to 25.

segments.title: Who must register and who is exempt
segments.summary: Men must register within 30 days of turning 18 up to age 26. Women are still not required to register even after combat roles opened. Exemption categories include service academy cadets, certain lawful nonimmigrants, and people institutionalized or confined. Penalties for failing to register include prosecution and withheld federal benefits and jobs.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short break in the episode.

segments.title: Draft lottery and induction process
segments.summary: If activated, a televised lottery pairs birth dates with numbers drawn from capsules. Men whose 20th birthdays fall on drawn dates are called first, and the call proceeds through age groups down to 18. Draftees report to a Regional Military Entrance Processing Station for physical and mental evaluation.

segments.title: Deferments and exemptions for students, ministers, and dependents
segments.summary: Draftees have ten days to file exemption claims. High school students and college students can postpone. Religious ministers, government officials, and men with dependents or hardship may get deferments.

segments.title: Conscientious objectors and alternative service
segments.summary: Conscientious objectors must be opposed to all war on moral, ethical, or religious grounds, not political grounds. Classifications 1-O and 1-O-dash-O distinguish combat objectors from those opposed to any military service. Those who qualify may be assigned to alternative service such as healthcare or conservation. Local boards of five civilian volunteers decide cases, and appeals are possible.

segments.title: Pros and cons of conscription and historical draft policy
segments.summary: The hosts debate the all-volunteer force against conscription, citing national unity, civic participation, and military professionalism. They discuss Lewis Hershey's deferment policy favoring middle-class white men in STEM fields, Robert McNamara's New Standards program that drafted about 354,000 men, many Black, and draftee casualties in Vietnam. They recommend Errol Morris's Fog of War and a New York Times op-ed by Amy J. Ruttenberg.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh reads an email from Noah in Scotland about the Shanghai Tower's tuned mass damper and the hosts sign off.
